explanation:
## The answer

```rust
fn settle(v: &mut [i64]) -> usize {
    let mid = v.len() / 2;
    let (left, right) = v.split_at_mut(mid);
    let mut swaps = 0;
    for i in 0..left.len() {
        if left[i] > right[i] {
            std::mem::swap(&mut left[i], &mut right[i]);
            swaps += 1;
        }
    }
    swaps
}
```

## Why the obvious version is refused

```rust
let left  = &mut v[..mid];
let right = &mut v[mid..];
```

Rust's rule is that at most one exclusive reference to a value may exist
at a time. The two expressions above both borrow `*v`, and the borrow
checker reasons about *which value* is borrowed, not about which range
of it — `[..mid]` and `[mid..]` are index expressions, and in general
index expressions can overlap.

That is not a limitation worth resenting. The alternative is a compiler
that tries to prove ranges disjoint, which works for literal constants
and fails for anything computed, and would therefore either reject real
code or accept aliasing it could not actually prove safe.

## What `split_at_mut` is

```rust
pub fn split_at_mut(&mut self, mid: usize) -> (&mut [T], &mut [T])
```

It takes **one** exclusive borrow and returns **two**, and it is sound
because the function itself guarantees the halves do not overlap — a
fact the type system cannot see but a human can check once, inside the
standard library, where it is implemented with raw pointers and an
`unsafe` block.

This is the pattern Rust uses everywhere the ownership rules are too
coarse: a small audited primitive with a safe signature, and everything
above it in safe code. `iter_mut`, `chunks_mut`, `split_first_mut` and
`Vec::drain` are all the same idea.

It panics if `mid > len`, which cannot happen here because `mid` is
`len / 2`.

## `mem::swap`

`std::mem::swap(&mut a, &mut b)` exchanges two values through two
exclusive references. It is the general form; within a single slice,
`v.swap(i, j)` is shorter and avoids the two borrows entirely by taking
the indices rather than references.

Either is better than the three-line version with a temporary, and for
a type that is not `Copy` the three-line version does not even compile:
moving out of `left[i]` would leave a hole in the slice, which Rust does
not allow. `mem::swap` works for every type because it never leaves one.

## The halves after the swaps

Each position is settled independently of every other. The sample
pairs left `5 1 9` against right `2 7 3`:

| i | before | after | swapped? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 5, 2 | 2, 5 | yes |
| 1 | 1, 7 | 1, 7 | no |
| 2 | 9, 3 | 3, 9 | yes |

which gives `left 2 1 3` and `right 5 7 9`, with two swaps.

Note what this is **not**: the halves do not come out sorted. Only the
smaller of each pair ends up on the left, and `2 1 3` is not in order.
Working out which element pairs with which before writing any code is
most of the exercise; pairing `left[i]` with `right[len-1-i]`, or
sorting afterwards, gives an answer that is self-consistent and not the
one asked for.
